class.name: AmbientProbeVolume3D
class.brief_description: Bakes large-scale ambient occlusion into a grid of probes filling a box volume, without lightmaps.
class.description: [AmbientProbeVolume3D] computes ambient occlusion (how exposed a point is to the sky/ambient light versus blocked by nearby geometry) at a regular grid of points filling the box defined by [member size] (centered on the node's origin), and stores one value per point. Pressing the [b]Bake AO[/b] button in the Inspector (or calling [method bake_ao]) does this entirely on the CPU by raycasting against the triangle geometry of every visible [MeshInstance3D] found under [member occluder_root] (or the current scene root if left unset) — plus, for nodes that don't carry a single [Mesh] of their own but still expose one the same way [LightmapGI] looks for it (currently [GridMap]), whatever mesh(es) that returns: for each probe, [member ray_count] rays are cast up to [member max_distance] in roughly uniform directions around the sphere, and the fraction that hit something becomes that probe's occlusion. [CSGShape3D] geometry is [i]not[/i] currently detected; convert it to a real mesh (e.g. via its own "Bake Mesh Instance" option) first if it should occlude. Every [method bake_ao] and [method apply_to_instances] call also prints a one-line summary to the Output panel (occluder triangle count found, or instance count affected) — check there first if a bake or an apply seems to have done nothing, before assuming something is broken. [method bake_ao] in particular also prints how far away the closest occluder triangle actually is from this volume's box: with a large scene (e.g. an architectural showcase like Sponza), the default [member size] and [member max_distance] are easy to leave too small/short for the scene's actual scale, in which case occluders are found but none of them are ever in reach of any probe — [method get_configuration_warnings] calls this out by name and suggests concrete numbers once that has happened. This is intentionally independent of [LightmapGI]/[LightmapProbe]: no mesh needs lightmap UV2s, nothing gets a baked lightmap texture, and no separate bake step for direct/indirect light is involved. It only ever produces ambient occlusion, which keeps baking fast and avoids forcing UV2 unwrapping (or lightmap texel budgeting) onto meshes—like scattered vegetation—that would be impractical to lightmap. If baked indirect [i]light[/i] (not just occlusion) is also wanted for some objects, use [LightmapGI]/[LightmapProbe] for those instead; the two systems don't conflict and can be used side by side. [b]Baking alone does not shade anything.[/b] This is the most common point of confusion: after [method bake_ao] runs, nothing in the scene looks any different yet, because nothing has been told to read the baked data. There are three ways to actually use it, in increasing order of manual effort: - Point [member FoliageSpawner3D.ambient_occlusion_volume] at this node. Its [method FoliageSpawner3D.regenerate] then samples [method get_ao_at] per instance and stores it in the generated [MultiMesh]'s per-instance custom data — but the mesh's shader still needs to read [code]INSTANCE_CUSTOM.r[/code] and use it (e.g. multiply it into [code]ALBEDO[/code] or [code]ALPHA[/code]); a default/[StandardMaterial3D] will not do this on its own. - Call [method apply_to_instances] (or press [b]Apply To Instances[/b] in the Inspector). This walks [member apply_target] (or the current scene root) and sets the [member apply_shader_parameter] per-instance shader parameter on every [GeometryInstance3D] found, to that instance's [method get_ao_at]. Just like above, this only has a visible effect on meshes whose own shader declares a matching [code]instance uniform float ambient_occlusion : hint_range(0, 1) = 1.0;[/code] and multiplies it into the shading somewhere; it does nothing by itself for a mesh using an unmodified [StandardMaterial3D]. - Call [method get_ao_at] directly from a script or a custom shader's own code for any other use (darkening a light's energy, driving a particle system, etc). In every case, some other code has to explicitly read [method get_ao_at] (or the data it feeds, such as [code]INSTANCE_CUSTOM[/code] or an instance shader parameter) and act on it — there is no project setting or material flag that makes arbitrary existing meshes pick this up automatically, unlike [VoxelGI], [SDFGI], or [LightmapGI], which the built-in [BaseMaterial3D]/[member Environment] rendering pipeline already knows how to sample. Consequently, there's also no separate "opt-out" needed for objects that shouldn't be affected (e.g. small props): simply don't apply it to them. To check whether a bake actually found any occlusion (as opposed to a setup issue, such as [member occluder_root] pointing at the wrong node, or [member max_distance] being too short to reach nearby geometry) without writing any code, select this node after baking: probes are drawn in the 3D viewport as small spheres tinted from white (fully lit) to black (fully occluded), similar to how Unity visualizes light probes. If every sphere stays white, nothing was actually occluded by the bake and the value is not the problem — see [method get_configuration_warnings] for a specific diagnosis. Before baking, the same probes are instead drawn as small crosses previewing where they will be placed. Either way, the per-probe preview only appears while this node is [i]selected[/i] (the box outline itself stays visible at all times so the volume can still be found/resized) — with dozens to thousands of probes, leaving them permanently drawn would clutter the viewport for every other object in the scene once a volume is baked. If the probe spheres [i]do[/i] show variation but the actual meshes still look untouched, that is not a bug: as explained above, nothing samples this data unless it's told to, and a plain [StandardMaterial3D] never will. To see the baked AO directly on the real geometry without writing a single line of shader code, enable [member debug_preview_on_meshes] (or press [b]Debug Preview On Meshes[/b] in the Inspector): every [GeometryInstance3D] under [member apply_target] gets a generated, fully unshaded material that renders it as flat grayscale by the baked AO at [i]each rendered fragment's[/i] world position, replacing whatever material it normally uses. Sampling per-fragment (rather than once per instance, like [method apply_to_instances] necessarily does) matters here: a scene with a handful of huge meshes — an entire imported building, for example — would otherwise show each mesh as one single flat tone, which looks exactly like "nothing is happening" even though the data is correct. This is a diagnostic override, not a shading technique meant to ship: turn it back off (same button/property) once you've confirmed the bake looks right, and then wire up [member FoliageSpawner3D.ambient_occlusion_volume] or a real shader using [member apply_shader_parameter]/[method get_ao_at] for the actual, permanent effect. [method get_configuration_warnings] reminds you if it's been left on. [b]VoxelGI vs. this node for large-scale ambient occlusion:[/b] [VoxelGI] voxelizes one fixed-resolution 3D texture (up to 256 per axis) across its whole box and updates in real time, which makes it a poor fit for very large or open outdoor areas: covering more world space either coarsens every voxel or spends a lot of GPU memory and bake/update time on a single volume, and its effect fades out near the box's edges. This node's probes are just points, placed wherever needed at whatever spacing is useful, with no such resolution-vs-coverage trade-off, and they cost nothing at runtime beyond [method get_ao_at]'s trilinear lookup (or, if pre-applied like [FoliageSpawner3D] and [method apply_to_instances] do, nothing at all). The trade-off is that baked data doesn't react to moving lights or geometry. For large, mostly-static outdoor scenes, prefer this node for ambient occlusion on vegetation and similar objects; reserve [VoxelGI] for smaller, bounded areas (e.g. a single interior or a gameplay-relevant room) where real-time reaction to moving lights matters. [SDFGI] (via [member Environment.sdfgi_enabled]) is usually a better real-time alternative to [VoxelGI] for large open worlds, since it works from cascades around the camera instead of a single fixed volume, but still costs GPU time every frame that baked data does not. [b]Note:[/b] [method bake_ao] and [method apply_to_instances] both require the node to be inside the [SceneTree], since they scan the scene tree.

method.name: apply_to_instances
method.description: Recursively walks [member apply_target] (or the current scene root if unset), and for every [GeometryInstance3D] found, sets its instance shader parameter named [member apply_shader_parameter] to [method get_ao_at] evaluated at that instance's position. See the class description for what the target's shader needs to declare for this to have any visible effect — if that hasn't been set up yet and you just want to confirm the bake looks right, use [member debug_preview_on_meshes] instead. Requires the volume to already be baked (see [method bake_ao]).

method.name: bake_ao
method.description: Scans [member occluder_root] (or the current scene root if unset) for occluder geometry (see the class description for exactly what counts), then raycasts from every probe in the [member probe_counts] grid filling [member size] to compute and store its ambient occlusion. Replaces any previously baked data. Prints the number of occluder triangles found, and how far the closest one is from this volume's box, to the Output panel; if the triangle count is [code]0[/code], or that distance is greater than [member max_distance], nothing will end up occluded no matter how [member ray_count] is tuned.

method.name: clear_ao
method.description: Discards any baked data. After this, [method get_ao_at] returns [code]1.0[/code] (fully lit) everywhere until [method bake_ao] is called again.

method.name: get_ao_at
method.description: Returns the baked ambient occlusion at [param world_position], trilinearly interpolated between the nearest probes ([code]1.0[/code] = fully lit, [code]0.0[/code] = fully occluded). Returns [code]1.0[/code] if [param world_position] is outside [member size], or if this volume hasn't been baked yet.

method.name: get_probe_ao
method.description: Returns the raw baked ambient occlusion of the probe at grid coordinates ([param x], [param y], [param z]) (each in the [code][0, probe_counts - 1][/code] range for the corresponding axis of [member probe_counts]), with no interpolation. Returns [code]1.0[/code] if the coordinates are out of range or this volume hasn't been baked yet. Mainly useful for inspecting or visualizing the bake directly (this is what the editor gizmo's probe spheres use); for shading, [method get_ao_at] is usually more convenient since it takes a world position.

method.name: is_baked
method.description: Returns [code]true[/code] if [method bake_ao] has been called since the last [method clear_ao] (or since [member probe_counts] last changed, which also clears baked data since it no longer matches the grid).

members.member: Multiplies how strongly hits reduce a probe's ambient occlusion during [method bake_ao]. Values above [code]1.0[/code] exaggerate occlusion (a probe can go fully dark from partial occlusion); [code]0.0[/code] disables the effect entirely (everything stays fully lit).

The name of the instance shader parameter that [method apply_to_instances] sets on every [GeometryInstance3D] it finds. A target's shader needs to declare a matching [code]instance uniform float [/code][i]name[/i][code] : hint_range(0, 1) = 1.0;[/code] to be affected.
The root node that [method apply_to_instances] scans (recursively) for [GeometryInstance3D] nodes. If left empty, the current scene root is used (the edited scene root in the editor).
Pressing this button in the Inspector calls [method apply_to_instances]. It is not meant to be read or assigned from code; use [method apply_to_instances] directly instead.
Pressing this button in the Inspector calls [method bake_ao]. It is not meant to be read or assigned from code; use [method bake_ao] directly instead.
Pressing this button in the Inspector calls [method clear_ao]. It is not meant to be read or assigned from code; use [method clear_ao] directly instead.

If [code]true[/code], every [GeometryInstance3D] under [member apply_target] (or the current scene root) has its [member GeometryInstance3D.material_override] replaced with a generated, unshaded material that renders it as flat grayscale by the baked AO, sampled per-fragment at that fragment's actual world position (via a 3D texture built from the bake) — a direct, code-free way to see the baked result on the actual geometry, with real spatial detail even across a single large mesh. See the class description for details. Setting this back to [code]false[/code] clears [member GeometryInstance3D.material_override] on every instance it finds; it does [i]not[/i] restore whatever override (if any) those instances had before this was turned on, so it is meant purely as a temporary diagnostic, not something to leave on.

The maximum ray length used by [method bake_ao], in meters. Geometry farther than this from a probe cannot occlude it. Larger values catch more distant occluders but increase bake time and tend to darken probes that are simply far from any surface (which is not always desired for ambient occlusion). The default is tuned for a human-sized scene; a much larger one (e.g. an imported architectural showcase) may need a proportionally larger value, or every probe will come back fully lit even with valid occluder geometry nearby — [method bake_ao]'s Output panel message and [method get_configuration_warnings] both call this out explicitly when it happens.
The root node that [method bake_ao] scans (recursively) for occluders (see the class description). If left empty, the current scene root is used (the edited scene root in the editor).

The number of probes along each axis, clamped between [code]1[/code] and [code]64[/code] per axis. The total probe count ([member probe_counts].x × [member probe_counts].y × [member probe_counts].z) directly affects [method bake_ao]'s running time, so keep it as low as the desired detail allows. Changing this clears any previously baked data, since it no longer matches the new grid.
The number of rays cast per probe by [method bake_ao], spread roughly uniformly over the sphere. Higher values produce smoother, less noisy occlusion at the cost of longer bake times.
The size of the box volume that probes fill, centered on the node's origin.
